schools.summary: Gill infers Elijah's foreknowledge from his movements and calls the school at Bethel a nursery for religion set up where a calf stood.

Henry asks why the honour fell to Elijah and answers by looking back, down and forward to Christ's ascension, prefers a trial of Elisha's constancy to modesty as the motive, and holds that the colleges supplied what Israel lacked in priests and temple.

Clarke has the translation revealed to Elijah, Elisha and both schools alike; Wesley adds a fourth motive for the dismissals and reads the taking from above the head of the schoolroom or of a power sent from heaven.

Ellicott rejects both standard motives for the dismissals in favour of Elijah's own uncertainty about God's will, identifies the Gilgal of the verse as the one in Ephraim, and sets aside Ewald's reason for the visit to Bethel; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the idiom and the purpose of the revelation.

debates.question: Why did Elijah keep urging Elisha to stay behind?

sides.position: Modesty, sparing Elisha grief, or a test of his knowledge and affection
Humility, or a trial that would make the adherence more commendable
That Elijah might be left alone to prepare for his change
Because Elijah did not know whether God willed Elisha to come; the threefold refusal settled it

debates.question: What does taking Elijah from above Elisha's head mean?

sides.position: A pictorial expression for his being raised from Elisha's side
The word stands for the person, or means from his position of superiority as master
The schoolroom, where a scholar sat at his master's feet, or a literal departure overhead

outliers.note: Alone in denying the two motives every other voice offers for the dismissals, and in grounding them instead on Elijah's own uncertainty whether God meant Elisha to accompany him.

themes: the Lord will take away thy master from thy head to day
as the Lord liveth, I will not leave thee
the sons of the prophets at Bethel
yea, I know it; hold ye your peace
1.pericope_label: The Lord will take away thy master from thee today: hold thy peace

schools.summary: Gill notes that Jericho, rebuilt under a curse on its builder, nevertheless held a school of the prophets, and reports the opinion that the mantle was a shorter shoulder robe rather than the hairy garment.

Clarke makes the skins dressed with the hair on the insignia of a prophet's office and traces the custom to university hoods and royal ermine, and calls the dividing a miracle possible only to almighty power; Wesley supplies the typology of the ark, the mantle and the Jordan of death.

Ellicott takes the verbatim repetition as evidence of oral transmission in the guilds, borrows from Reuss a description of the mood, and explains why the fifty posted themselves where they did; Keil and Delitzsch find a purpose in the route and make the cloak the vehicle of the power.

debates.question: Why did fifty of the sons of the prophets follow at a distance?

sides.position: To get a view of the assumption and be witnesses of it
Not from curiosity but so that they might testify of it to others
To see whether and how their master would cross where there was no ford

outliers.note: Alone in drawing a text-critical inference from the form of the narrative, that the exchange repeated word for word at each stage points to transmission by oral tradition within the prophetic guilds.

themes: the Lord hath sent me to Jericho
fifty men stood to view afar off
he took his mantle, and wrapped it together
they were divided hither and thither
4.pericope_label: He took his mantle and smote the waters, and they were divided

schools.summary: Gill makes the thing asked a rare privilege, seldom enjoyed and hard to obtain.
Henry borrows Bishop Hall's observation on asking before the departure rather than after, marks what Elisha did not request, and takes the word hard as teaching him to value the gift.

Clarke grounds the double portion in the law of the firstborn and renders the Hebrew as two parts rather than twice the quantity, and will not let the promise hang on the bare act of seeing; Wesley holds the gift exceeded the asking.

Ellicott states the wrong interpretation in order to reject it and makes the request a claim to be the true spiritual heir; Keil and Delitzsch catalogue the misreading from Ephraem Syrus to Krummacher.

debates.question: What did Elisha mean by a double portion of the spirit?

sides.position: The firstborn's share, twice what any other disciple would have
Double what the rest of the prophets had, not double Elijah's own measure
Not twice Elijah's own endowment, which is the reading of Ephraem Syrus, Luther and others

debates.question: What was the force of the condition about seeing Elijah taken away?

sides.position: Not the bare act of seeing, which no divine gift could hang on, but continuing with him to the end
A test of worthiness, implying also that the departure would be above ordinary perception
A sign proposed to engage Elisha to wait and pray more earnestly
Both the condition and the means, close attendance to the last being what obtains the spirit

outliers.note: Alone in separating the asking from the outcome, holding that God gave more than was desired, so that Elisha seems to have had a greater portion of the Spirit's gifts than Elijah himself.

themes: ask what I shall do for thee
let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me
thou hast asked a hard thing
if thou see me when I am taken from thee
9.pericope_label: Let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me: thou hast asked a hard thing

schools.summary: Gill reads the seeing as the token securing the double portion and finds the whole scene answering closely to the ascension of Christ.

Clarke insists on the plain sense in order to shut out Priestley's conjecture about the translated living in this world; Wesley takes the chariot for the visible form of an angelic guard, Elijah having his body to carry with him.

Ellicott makes the word a storm-blast and the fiery car a popular notion read into the text, citing Bähr and Von Gerlach and noting that the ascension is nowhere else mentioned in scripture; Keil and Delitzsch make it a tempest with a fiery phenomenon that appeared to Elisha as a chariot.

debates.question: How literally is the chariot of fire to be taken?

sides.position: Literally: the angels appeared in that form so that Elijah might ride in state
Literally, and the text leaves no room for conjecture about where the translated now are
A tempest accompanied by a fiery phenomenon which appeared to Elisha's eyes as a chariot
A storm theophany; the fiery car drawn by horses is read into the text rather than gathered from it

outliers.note: Alone in arguing the ascension down to a storm theophany, naming Blake's picture as the popular conception, and adding that Elijah's being taken into heaven is nowhere alluded to in the rest of the Bible.

themes: a chariot of fire, and horses of fire
Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven
my father, my father
the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof
11.pericope_label: A chariot of fire and horses of fire: the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof

schools.summary: Gill makes the fallen mantle the token of succession and of the double portion.

Henry has Elijah let fall his mantle instead of his body, warns that Elisha took it as a garment to wear and not a relic to worship, and makes Elijah's last miracle Elisha's first so that there is no vacancy.
Clarke reports and dismantles the Latin reading that makes the first smiting fail; Wesley has God order the fall for the strengthening of Elisha's faith.

Ellicott says outright that something is wrong in the doubled clause and canvasses Keil, Thenius, Houbigant and two conjectures of his own; Keil and Delitzsch make the mantle a pledge to Elisha and a sign to others.

debates.question: How is the doubled clause about smiting the waters to be explained?

sides.position: The Latin makes it two strikings, the first failing; but no other version follows it and the Hebrew lacks the clause
The two words belong to the question, giving where is the God of Elijah, even he
Houbigant's correction gives where then, Thenius thinking Keil's use doubtful
Either the word where was repeated for emphasis, or the words should be transposed to give he smote, he also

outliers.note: Alone in reading the use of the mantle as a declaration of method, that Elisha meant to keep to his master's ways and introduce nothing new, unlike those who think themselves wiser than their predecessors.

themes: he took up also the mantle of Elijah
where is the Lord God of Elijah?
they parted hither and thither
Elisha went over
13.pericope_label: He took up the mantle of Elijah: where is the Lord God of Elijah?

schools.summary: Gill identifies the watchers as those who had gone out from Jericho and takes the shame to be shame at refusing them longer.

Clarke thinks the fifty strong men the same fifty who saw the ascension and supposes they allowed the Spirit might have set Elijah down on a mountain; Wesley offers two motives for the search and explains the shame by fear of seeming to neglect his master.

Ellicott leaves open whether the watchers are the fifty or the whole guild, rejects Keil's motive for the search, reports a Greek reading that has Elijah cast into the Jordan, and closes the history with Reuss and Thenius; Keil and Delitzsch put the request down to an inability to realise the translation.

debates.question: Why did the sons of the prophets want to search for Elijah?

sides.position: They could not realise the fact of the translation though it had been revealed to them
They allowed he had gone up but thought the Spirit might have set him down on a mountain or in a valley
Either God had taken him only for a time, or only his soul, the body being left to be buried honourably
They expected to find him alive, so the motive was not burial as Keil suggests

debates.question: What does it mean that they urged him until he was ashamed?

sides.position: Shame at denying them any longer
The awkwardness of a man who cannot decently hold out against importunity
Embarrassed and put out of countenance, or on other views shamelessly pressed, or disappointed of dissuading them

outliers.note: Alone in turning the search request into evidence about the ascension itself, since men who proposed to look for Elijah on the hills cannot have seen him ride visibly into heaven in a fiery car.

themes: the spirit of Elijah doth rest on Elisha
let them go and seek thy master
they urged him till he was ashamed
did I not say unto you, Go not?
15.pericope_label: Let them go and seek thy master: ye shall not send

schools.summary: Gill has the new vessel chosen so that no one could credit the virtue to anything previously in it, and carries the healing down through Josephus and modern travellers to a spring still called Elisha's fountain.

Henry reasons from the smallness of the quantity that the means were nothing and the trial of faith everything, draws the moral that the spring was treated and so the streams, and sets the miracle in the history of a city built in defiance of a threat.

Clarke makes the barren ground the effect of the bad water and quotes Jarchi that salt corrupts water, so the miracle is evident; Wesley calls salt a most improper remedy, chosen to show that God can work without means or against them.
Ellicott insists the citizens and not the prophets brought the complaint, denies that barren land is a correct translation, and makes the salt an antiseptic and so an appropriate sacramental medium.

debates.question: What was the evil complained of at Jericho?

sides.position: Barren soil, caused by the badness of the water
Barrenness either original or inflicted by the curse on the city's rebuilder
Not the soil at all: the land stands for its inhabitants and their animals, and the sense is miscarriage, so barren land is an incorrect translation

debates.question: Was salt a fit means for healing the spring?

sides.position: No: salt makes water brackish and land barren, so it was chosen to show that God works without means or against them
Yes: as an antiseptic it was an appropriate sacramental medium for expelling the corruption
The quantity settles it; so small a measure could do nothing, the point being the trial of faith and obedience

outliers.note: Alone in rejecting the received translation of the complaint, holding that the word rendered barren land means the multiplying of miscarriage among the inhabitants and their animals, and that this is no popular superstition as Reuss supposes.

themes: the water is naught, and the ground barren
bring me a new cruse, and put salt therein
thus saith the Lord, I have healed these waters
the waters were healed unto this day
19.pericope_label: Bring me a new cruse, and put salt therein: I have healed these waters

schools.summary: Gill has Elisha turn with a stern countenance to shame the mockers, to no purpose, and reckons the distance from Bethel to Carmel at fifty-six miles.

Clarke argues from usage that young men and not little children are meant, shifts the agency of the judgment wholly to God, and conjectures that the forty-two had themselves destroyed the whelps of these same bears; Wesley makes the taunt a settled scoff from rooted impiety rather than a slip of the tongue.

Ellicott allows the mockers any age up to twenty, denies that the taunt refers to Elijah's ascension at all, and notes that baldness was suspect as a mark of leprosy; Keil and Delitzsch answer the charge of immorality in the cursing and refuse the expedient of a plot by the city's rulers.

debates.question: What did the taunt go up mean?

sides.position: Ascend to heaven as it is pretended thy master did; blasphemy against God
Not that at all, since the Bethelites knew no more of the ascension than the men of Jericho; it refers to Elisha climbing the steep road at that moment

debates.question: How is the curse and its outcome to be justified?

sides.position: The charge of immorality, if established, would fall back on God who executed it; no plot by the rulers need be supposed
Elisha had no power to bring bears, so the curse was only declaratory of what God was about to do
The bears may have been pursuing the same young men for destroying their whelps, God's justice guiding them to the spot

outliers.note: Alone in offering a naturalistic reconstruction, that the forty-two may have been the very young men who had destroyed these she-bears' whelps, so that the beasts were already prepared by their loss to execute the curse.

themes: go up, thou bald head
he cursed them in the name of the Lord
two she bears out of the wood
he went from thence to mount Carmel
23.pericope_label: There came forth two she bears out of the wood
